claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be processed into an initially homogeneous, single-phase high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between a thermodynamic driving force for chemical ordering and kinetic limitations from sluggish solute diffusion.
The thermodynamic tendency toward ordering mainly arises from unfavorable mixing enthalpies between Al and certain transition metals.
Al and Cr are notable contributors to sluggish solute diffusion in this alloy.
At high temperature, configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered BCC structure.
Cooling increases the free-energy benefit of forming chemically short-range-ordered clusters.
Limited diffusivity delays nucleation of a new ordered phase.
Localized chemical short-range order involves Al–Cr clustering or Al depletion around Co, Fe, and Ni.
Localized chemical short-range order acts as a precursor to nucleation of an ordered secondary phase or intermetallic precipitate.
During slow cooling, diffusion becomes sufficient for ordered clusters to form and lower the alloy free energy.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and kinetically freezes the high-temperature disordered BCC state.
Slow cooling or isothermal annealing will produce more chemical ordering or secondary-phase formation than rapid quenching.
The rapidly quenched baseline will remain largely single-phase, disordered BCC.
Ordering or phase separation can be detected through secondary diffraction peaks, ordered TEM domains, or local segregation and short-range order measured by atom-probe tomography.
The extent of ordering or secondary-phase formation will depend on cooling rate and annealing time.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately between 900°C and 1200°C, where atomic mobility begins to permit diffusion.
The comparison holds composition and prior processing history constant while varying the cooling or holding schedule.
A lack of detectable differences in phase composition and local chemical order between quenched and slowly cooled samples would falsify the proposed competition mechanism.
